title: Capturing the daylight dividend in buildings: why and how?

findings.consequent: Interesting, dynamic interiors supportive of human health and activities
findings.quote: Done properly, daylighting creates interesting, dynamic interiors supportive of human health and activities while reducing energy demand.

findings.consequent: Building energy demand
findings.quote: Done properly, daylighting creates interesting, dynamic interiors supportive of human health and activities while reducing energy demand.

findings.consequent: Vision impairment, discomfort, excessive energy demand
findings.quote: Done improperly, it impedes vision, causes discomfort, and demands excessive energy.

findings.consequent: Economic benefits (beyond energy savings)
findings.quote: Current research results are leading to a realization of broader economic benefits from daylighting, a dividend that may strongly justify initial construction expenses.

findings.consequent: Electric energy consumption
findings.quote: Energy is not saved by daylighting; energy is saved by dimming down or switching off electric lights that are not needed because of daylight. Daylighting case studies report energy savings of as much as 52% along the window wall [1].

findings.consequent: Air conditioning energy requirements (due to reduced internal cooling load from lights)
findings.quote: Daylighting often reduces air conditioning energy requirements as well because the internal cooling load from the lights is reduced.

findings.consequent: Power plant emissions (acid rain, air pollution, global warming)
findings.quote: Electric energy savings also result in fewer power plant emissions that contribute to acid rain, air pollution, and global warming.

findings.consequent: Potential for additional energy savings from daylighting
findings.quote: Because new office lighting systems may demand as little power as 10 W/m² (1 W/sf²), the potential for energy savings from daylight is lower now than with older, inefficient electric lighting systems.

findings.consequent: Electricity demand charges and peak load
findings.quote: However, maximum daylight availability often coincides with building peak energy demand during the afternoon of sunny days. Therefore, daylighting can lower electricity demand charges... Peak load reductions realized through daylighting reduce demand for power when supplies are often met by less environmentally friendly power sources.

findings.consequent: Worker productivity, job satisfaction, reduced absenteeism
findings.quote: Therefore, the strongest economic argument for daylighting may be the worker's improved productivity, increased job satisfaction, or reduced absenteeism, each of which can easily offset an initial investment in daylight systems.

findings.consequent: Ability to continue working on some tasks during power outages
findings.quote: Daylight allows people to continue working on some tasks during power outages.

findings.consequent: Perception of healthy buildings, indoor environmental quality, and status
findings.quote: People care about so-called green buildings and associate daylighting with healthy buildings and indoor environmental quality. They have a strong preference for windows in their offices [2,3] and believe windows improve their productivity.

findings.consequent: Visual information (weather, time, activities), aesthetic pleasure, respite from focused work
findings.quote: View gives the occupant visual information about weather, time of day, and surrounding activities. Views also can be aesthetically pleasing and give a respite from closely focused work. People deprived of view increase the images of nature on their office walls [4].

findings.consequent: Interesting, enlivening lighting effects ('light chords')
findings.quote: A good daylighting design can use these changing properties to create interesting lighting effects that modulate throughout the day and year. These special effects, termed 'light chords', enliven our indoor environments with special luminous events [5].

findings.consequent: Ease of seeing visual tasks, performance
findings.quote: It is well understood that more light makes it easier to see visual tasks. More light will improve performance, although with rapidly decreasing impact once one is above the recommended level.

findings.consequent: Higher indoor light levels (than economically provided by electric light alone)
findings.quote: A great benefit of daylight is that it allows our buildings to be lit at higher levels than with electric lighting alone.

findings.consequent: Broad electromagnetic spectrum, excellent color rendering
findings.quote: Daylight provides a broad electromagnetic spectrum with excellent color rendering, although electric light can, at a price, provide equal color rendering.

findings.consequent: Retail sales
findings.quote: A 1999 study, for example, reports a correlation between skylights and higher retail sales [7].

findings.consequent: Reduced human performance, fatigue, mood shifts (e.g., SAD), jet lag symptoms
findings.quote: People spending the day in non-daylit buildings may therefore be in 'biological darkness', contributing to reduced performance. Disruption of the intensity, duration, or time of exposure to light, may indeed contribute to fatigue, mood shifts such as Seasonal Affective Disorder, and reduced performance commonly associated with jet lag.

findings.consequent: Occupant discomfort
findings.quote: Fenestration must avoid excessive solar heat gain resulting in occupant discomfort.

findings.consequent: Glare, degradation of fabric/artwork, interference with AV equipment, lack of privacy
findings.quote: The brightness and distribution of the sunlight must be controlled to avoid glare and minimize degradation of fabric, artwork, and other light-sensitive objects. Windows must be controlled to avoid interference with audio-visual equipment and to afford privacy when desired.

findings.consequent: Light penetration depth into space
findings.quote: Windows higher on the wall will allow the light to penetrate further into the space.

findings.consequent: Uniformity and balanced brightness within a room
findings.quote: Admit daylight from more than one side of a space where possible. Bilateral lighting, for example, increases uniformity and balances the brightness within the room.

findings.consequent: Luminance contrast between windows and surrounding surfaces, visual comfort
findings.quote: Light surfaces reduce the luminance contrast between the windows and surrounding surfaces, increasing visual comfort.

findings.antecedent: Workstations and computer screens perpendicular to windows
findings.consequent: Reflected glare in screens, visual discomfort
findings.quote: Locate workstations and computer screens perpendicular to the windows to reduce reflected glare in the screens or visual discomfort.

findings.consequent: Daylight zone depth
findings.quote: Light shelves... reflect sunlight onto a light-colored ceiling, increasing the daylight zone by a few meters under sunny conditions.

findings.consequent: Daylight zone depth
findings.quote: Buildings with high windows and high ceilings have extended daylight zones as well.

findings.antecedent: Adjusted horizontal blinds (directing sun to ceiling)
findings.consequent: Daylight penetration depth, view maintenance, excessive brightness on work tasks
findings.quote: Horizontal blinds adjusted to direct sunlight to the ceiling also increase the depth of daylight penetration, maintain a view, and reduce excessive brightness on work tasks. Frequently, however, blinds or shades are pulled to eliminate direct sun and not readjusted after the Sun's position has changed. Window blinds can easily occlude more than half of the available daylight on the east, south, and west facades [11].

findings.consequent: Perceived dimness of interior space, electric light use, energy savings from daylight
findings.quote: Glass with very low transmission, however, may be unacceptable to occupants [12]. If the resulting interior space appears dim, occupants may add more electric light, further reducing any energy savings from daylight.

findings.consequent: Perceived enhanced brightness, visual task performance
findings.quote: Certain tints of glass give the appearance of enhanced brightness. Bronze glass, for example, can make a view appear significantly brighter than the same view seen through blue-tinted glass with the same transmittance. People will feel the space is brighter, although there is no improvement in visual task performance [13].

findings.antecedent: Skylights, roof monitors, clerestory windows, translucent roofs
findings.consequent: Daylighting areas beyond the perimeter zone (top floor)
findings.quote: For the top floor, skylights, roof monitors, clerestory windows, and translucent roofs are used to light areas beyond the perimeter zone.

findings.antecedent: Atria/light wells (vertical spaces exposed to sky)
findings.consequent: Daylighting deep core buildings
findings.quote: Vertical spaces within the building's footprint that are exposed to the sky... create an internal perimeter that can be daylit. Light wells are not effective in delivering substantial daylight in adjacent building space beyond a few stories [14].

findings.consequent: Economic viability for general-purpose lighting
findings.quote: Beam daylighting systems using optics to convey sunlight deep into the core of buildings [10,15]... are not economically viable for general-purpose lighting.

findings.consequent: Energy savings from daylighting
findings.quote: Controls are the key to energy savings when using daylighting [17]. Switch sticker reminders to turn off lights, coupled with encouragement from management, may be more cost effective than automatic daylight control systems [18]. Manual dimming can also be an effective energy-savings strategy in private offices [19].

findings.consequent: Shortened lamp life, reduced confidence in dimming systems
findings.quote: Incompatibility of certain dimming ballasts with certain lamps have led to shortened lamp life and reduced confidence of lighting system specifiers in dimming systems.

findings.consequent: Difficulty in commissioning, effectiveness in saving energy in automatically controlled daylight systems
findings.quote: Photosensors... have been difficult to commission and are the weak link in saving energy in an automatically controlled daylight system [20].

findings.consequent: Improved daylight dimming systems
findings.quote: The recent development of a self-commissioning photosensor technology offers hope for improved daylight dimming systems.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to daylight levels (for a portion of each morning)
findings.consequent: Alertness, sleep quality, productivity
findings.quote: the research on photobiological effects of light suggests that people may be more alert, sleep better at night, and perhaps be more productive when they are exposed to daylight levels for at least a portion of each morning.
